concepts.title: Definition of AP and Common Difference
concepts.definition: An Arithmetic Progression (AP) is a list of numbers in which each term is obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding term. This fixed number is called the common difference (d) of the AP. An AP is written as a, a+d, a+2d, a+3d, ... where a is the first term and d is the common difference.
concepts.key_idea: The common difference d is the same between any two consecutive terms. It can be positive, negative, or zero.

solution_steps.explain: Take the first term and the term that follows it.

solution_steps.action: Subtract to get the common difference
solution_steps.explain: d equals the later term minus the earlier term.

worked_examples.question: Find the common difference of the AP: 3, 6, 9, 12, ...
worked_examples.solution: a_1 = 3, a_2 = 6, a_3 = 9. d = a_2 - a_1 = 6 - 3 = 3. Check: a_3 - a_2 = 9 - 6 = 3. Common difference is constant.

worked_examples.question: Write the first four terms of an AP where a = 5 and d = -3.
Is the sequence 2, 4, 8, 16, ... an AP?
worked_examples.solution: a_2 - a_1 = 4 - 2 = 2; a_3 - a_2 = 8 - 4 = 4. The differences are not equal, so it is not an AP.

concepts.title: nth Term of an AP
concepts.definition: The nth term of an AP with first term a and common difference d is given by the formula a_n = a + (n-1)*d. This is also called the general term of the AP.
concepts.key_idea: The nth term formula lets you find any term of an AP without listing all previous terms. It is also used to check whether a given number is a term of the AP.

concepts.title: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
concepts.definition: The sum of the first n terms of an AP with first term a and common difference d is given by S_n = n/2 * (2a + (n-1)*d). This formula is useful when the first term and common difference are known.
concepts.key_idea: The sum formula gives the total of the first n terms directly without listing all terms. It is derived from pairing terms from the start and end of the AP.

concepts.title: Sum of AP with Given First and Last Term
concepts.definition: When the first term a and the last term l of an AP are known, the sum of the first n terms is given by S_n = n/2 * (a + l). This is an alternative form of the sum formula.
concepts.key_idea: This formula is useful when the last term is known or easier to find than the common difference. It is equivalent to S_n = n/2 * (2a + (n-1)*d) since l = a + (n-1)*d.

concepts.title: Finding Missing Terms in an AP
concepts.definition: When some terms of an AP are missing, they can be found using the property that the common difference is constant. If two non-consecutive terms are known, use a_n = a + (n-1)*d to find a and d, then compute the missing terms.
concepts.key_idea: The common difference can be found from any two known terms using d = (a_m - a_n)/(m - n). Once d is known, all missing terms can be computed.

solution_steps.explain: d = (a_m - a_n) / (m - n); the position gap is at least 1.

concepts.title: Word Problems on AP
concepts.definition: Word problems on AP involve real-life situations that can be modeled as arithmetic progressions, such as savings, distances, salaries, and arrangements. The key is to identify the first term, common difference, and the quantity to find.
concepts.key_idea: Translate the word problem into AP parameters: the first value is a, the constant change is d, and the position or total is n. Then apply the appropriate AP formula.

solution_steps.explain: Starting value becomes a, the fixed change becomes d and the count becomes n.
Half of n times (2a + (n - 1)d).

concepts.title: Verifying an Arithmetic Progression
concepts.definition: A sequence is an AP if and only if the difference between any two consecutive terms is constant. To verify, compute a_(n+1) - a_n for all consecutive pairs and check if the difference is the same throughout.
concepts.formula: Check: a_2 - a_1 = a_3 - a_2 = ... = a_(n+1) - a_n = d (constant)
concepts.key_idea: If the common difference is the same for every pair of consecutive terms, the sequence is an AP. Any single pair with a different difference means it is not an AP.
question_patterns: Verify whether a given finite sequence is an AP
Verify whether a sequence defined by a formula a_n = f(n) is an AP

solution_steps.explain: Subtract each term from the next (or compute a_(n+1) - a_n from the formula).
Every difference must equal the same constant d.
A constant d confirms an AP; unequal differences mean it is not an AP.

worked_examples.question: Verify whether the sequence 5, 9, 13, 17, 21 is an AP.
worked_examples.solution: Differences: 9 - 5 = 4, 13 - 9 = 4, 17 - 13 = 4, 21 - 17 = 4. All differences are equal to 4.
worked_examples.answer: Yes, it is an AP with common difference d = 4

worked_examples.question: Verify whether the sequence defined by a_n = 3n + 2 is an AP.
worked_examples.solution: a_n = 3n + 2, a_(n+1) = 3(n+1) + 2 = 3n + 5. a_(n+1) - a_n = (3n + 5) - (3n + 2) = 3, which is constant for all n.
worked_examples.answer: Yes, it is an AP with common difference d = 3

worked_examples.question: Verify whether the sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 is an AP.
worked_examples.solution: Differences: 4 - 1 = 3, 9 - 4 = 5, 16 - 9 = 7, 25 - 16 = 9. The differences are not equal.
worked_examples.answer: No, it is not an AP

concepts.title: Finding the nth Term from the End of an AP
concepts.definition: The nth term from the end of an AP with first term a, common difference d, and last term l can be found by reversing the AP. In the reversed AP, the last term becomes the first term and the common difference becomes -d.
concepts.formula: nth term from end = l - (n - 1) * d ; where l is the last term
concepts.key_idea: Treat the AP in reverse order: the last term l becomes the first term, and the common difference becomes -d. Then the nth term from the end is l + (n-1)*(-d) = l - (n-1)*d.

solution_steps.explain: Take the last term, the common difference and the position counted from the end.

concepts.title: Sum and Terms of an AP
concepts.definition: The sum of the first n terms of an AP and the nth term are related by the formula: a_n = S_n - S_(n-1). That is, the nth term equals the difference between the sum of the first n terms and the sum of the first (n-1) terms.
concepts.key_idea: If the sum S_n is given as a function of n, the nth term can be found by computing S_n - S_(n-1). Conversely, if a_n is known, S_n can be found by summation. This relationship is fundamental for problems where the sum is given as an expression in n.
